title: How do you implement blue-green deployments in an API Gateway (weighted routing)?
shortTitle: How to implement blue-green deployments in an API Gateway

s1_definition.profdef: A blue-green deployment runs two complete production environments, the current version called blue and the new version called green, and switches traffic from one to the other. At the gateway, this is implemented with weighted routing: the gateway sends a configurable percentage of traffic to blue and green, starting at one hundred percent blue, then shifting weight toward green, and finally cutting over fully to green. Because both environments are live and the shift is controlled by route weights, you can move gradually, watch metrics, and instantly roll back by shifting weight back to blue if green misbehaves.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India opens a brand-new banking hall, the green hall, right next to the existing one, the blue hall, both fully staffed and ready. The manager stands at the entrance directing customers. At first he sends everyone to the trusted blue hall. Then he quietly sends a few customers to the green hall and watches whether they are served well. If green works, he sends more and more, until finally everyone goes to green and blue is closed. If anything goes wrong in green, he instantly waves all customers back to blue. The manager directing customers by proportion is the gateway doing weighted routing.
s1_definition.oneliner: Blue-green runs old and new side by side and uses gateway weighted routing to shift traffic gradually from blue to green, with instant rollback by shifting the weights back.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A blue-green deployment runs two complete production environments, the current version called blue and the new version called green, and switches traffic from one to the other. At the gateway, this is implemented with weighted routing: the gateway sends a configurable percentage of traffic to blue and green, starting at one hundred percent blue, then shifting weight toward green, and finally cutting over fully to green. Because both environments are live and the shift is controlled by route weights, you can move gradually, watch metrics, and instantly roll back by shifting weight back to blue if green misbehaves.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India opens a brand-new banking hall, the green hall, right next to the existing one, the blue hall, both fully staffed and ready. The manager stands at the entrance directing customers. At first he sends everyone to the trusted blue hall. Then he quietly sends a few customers to the green hall and watches whether they are served well. If green works, he sends more and more, until finally everyone goes to green and blue is closed. If anything goes wrong in green, he instantly waves all customers back to blue. The manager directing customers by proportion is the gateway doing weighted routing.

**One line to remember:** Blue-green runs old and new side by side and uses gateway weighted routing to shift traffic gradually from blue to green, with instant rollback by shifting the weights back.

sections.s2_technical:
The foundation of blue-green is that both versions are fully deployed and healthy at the same time. Blue is the current version serving all traffic; green is the new version, fully running but receiving little or no traffic yet. Because green is already deployed, the "release" is just a traffic decision, not a deployment, which is what makes cutover and rollback so fast.

Weighted routing is the gateway mechanism that makes the traffic decision. The gateway holds two routes for the same path, one to blue and one to green, each with a weight. When a request matches the path, the gateway picks blue or green in proportion to their weights. Spring Cloud Gateway provides a Weight route predicate for exactly this, for example two routes in the same weight group where blue has weight ninety and green weight ten sends roughly ten percent of traffic to green.

The rollout is a sequence of weight changes. You start at blue one hundred, green zero. You shift to blue ninety, green ten and watch green's error rate, latency, and business metrics. If healthy, you continue to fifty-fifty, then to green one hundred. Each step is a small, reversible change, and because routing is dynamic, each step takes effect without redeploying anything. The final step, green one hundred, is the full cutover, after which blue can be retired or kept as the instant rollback target.

Rollback is the key safety property. If green shows errors at any weight, you shift the weight back toward blue, often straight back to blue one hundred, and the problem disappears immediately because blue never stopped working. There is no need to redeploy or rebuild; the fix is a route-weight change, which can be done in seconds.

Session and state concerns matter. Pure blue-green assumes requests can go to either version, which is cleanest when services are stateless and the two versions share compatible data. If green introduces a database schema change, you must make it backward compatible so blue and green can both read and write during the overlap, typically using expand-and-contract migrations. Sticky routing, where a given user stays on one color for consistency, can be layered on with a routing key, but it complicates rollback.

A senior nuance is the distinction from canary and from rolling updates. Blue-green keeps two full environments and switches between them, favoring fast, clean cutover and rollback at the cost of running double capacity briefly. A canary is similar in using weights but emphasizes exposing a small user slice to a new version for observation, often with automated analysis. A rolling update replaces instances gradually within one environment and does not keep a full standby. Another nuance is that the weight changes should be driven through an audited, automated pipeline, because in a bank an accidental shift of payment traffic to a broken green must be prevented and must be instantly reversible.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India is releasing a new version of its account service. The team wants to release it without downtime and with the ability to undo instantly if something is wrong, because any disruption to balance lookups during business hours is unacceptable. Blue-green with weighted routing lets them shift traffic gradually and roll back in seconds.

Problem 2 — During the shift, both blue and green must be able to serve the same customer correctly, and if green's error rate rises, the gateway must move traffic back to blue immediately without any redeploy.

The connection to the fix: we will build a weighted router holding blue and green routes for the account path. We will simulate a rollout by changing the weights step by step, sending a batch of requests at each step and observing the split. We will then simulate green developing errors and roll back by resetting the weights to blue, showing traffic instantly returning to the healthy version.

What the code will do. There is a `Backend` enum of BLUE and GREEN. There is a `WeightedRoute` holding a blue weight and a green weight. There is a `BlueGreenRouter` that picks a backend per request by weight and can be reconfigured at runtime. There is an `AccountService` simulation per color, where green can be toggled to fail. There is a `DeploymentController` that performs the rollout steps and the rollback. The demo runs the full progression: all blue, ten percent green, fifty-fifty, all green, then green fails and we roll back to blue.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run the plain-Java blue-green demo
javac BlueGreenDemo.java
java com.bank.gateway.demo.BlueGreenDemo

# Real Spring Cloud Gateway: shift weights at runtime via actuator, then refresh
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/actuator/gateway/routes/account-green \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"uri":"lb://account-service-green","predicates":[{"name":"Path","args":{"pattern":"/api/v1/accounts/**"}},{"name":"Weight","args":{"group":"account-group","weight":"50"}}]}'
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/actuator/gateway/refresh
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is five batches of ten account requests as the deployment progresses, then an incident and a rollback.

Step 1. The router starts at blue one hundred, green zero. Every request in the first batch picks blue, because green has zero weight. All ten are served by the trusted current version. Nothing is exposed to green yet.

Step 2. The weights change to blue ninety, green ten. Now each request rolls against the combined weight, so roughly one in ten picks green. The batch shows about nine blue and one green. The team watches green's behavior on this small slice; because it is healthy, they continue. This change was just a weight update, no redeploy.

Step 3. The weights change to fifty-fifty. Now about half the batch goes to each color. Green is handling substantial real traffic correctly, which builds confidence. Both environments are live and serving the same customers interchangeably.

Step 4. The weights change to blue zero, green one hundred, the full cutover. Every request now picks green. The new version is serving all traffic, and blue is idle but still running, ready as a rollback target. The release is effectively complete.

Step 5. An incident strikes: green starts failing. The next batch shows errors coming from green. The team rolls back simply by setting the weights to blue one hundred, green zero. Because blue never stopped running, traffic instantly returns to the healthy version and the errors vanish, as the final healthy batch confirms. The rollback was a weight change that took effect in seconds, with no rebuild and no downtime.


sections.s6_takeaway:
A blue-green deployment runs two complete production environments at the same time, the current version called blue and the new version called green, and releases by switching traffic from one to the other. At the gateway I implement this with weighted routing: I keep two routes for the same path, one to blue and one to green, each with a weight, and the gateway picks a backend in proportion to those weights. Because both environments are already fully deployed and healthy, the release is just a traffic decision, which is what makes both the cutover and the rollback extremely fast.

The rollout is a sequence of small weight changes. I start at blue one hundred, green zero, so everything goes to the trusted version. Then I shift to blue ninety, green ten and watch green's error rate, latency, and business metrics on that small slice. If it is healthy, I move to fifty-fifty, then finally to green one hundred, which is the full cutover. In my banking work at National Bank of India, this is how we released a new account service with no downtime, because at every step both versions could serve the same customer and each step took effect through a route-weight change rather than a redeploy.

The property that makes blue-green worth it is instant rollback. In one release, green started throwing errors after the cutover, and we rolled back simply by setting the weights to blue one hundred, green zero. Because blue had never stopped running, traffic returned to the healthy version in seconds and the errors disappeared, with no rebuild and no outage. That safety net is the whole point: a bad release is undone by a weight change, not a deployment.

The nuances I always raise are data compatibility and how blue-green differs from its cousins. During the overlap, blue and green must both be able to read and write the shared data, so any schema change has to be backward compatible, which I do with expand-and-contract migrations. And I distinguish the strategies clearly: blue-green keeps two full environments and switches between them, favoring clean, fast cutover and rollback at the cost of briefly running double capacity; a canary also uses weights but focuses on exposing a small real-user slice for observation, often with automated analysis; and a rolling update replaces instances gradually within one environment without a full standby. In a bank, I also insist the weight changes run through an audited, automated pipeline, so an accidental shift of payment traffic to a broken green is prevented and always instantly reversible.
